title: Strategies vs Principles
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Jamie Lee Clark argues that effective teaching begins not with strategies but with principles—the underlying learning mechanisms that strategies are designed to enact. A strategy is the visible teaching action (cold calling, exit tickets, hinge questions); a principle is why you do it (teaching should respond to evidence of student thinking). Drawing on Dr. Haili Hughes' 2026 article 'The De-intellectualisation of Teaching,' Clark warns that when strategies are mandated without teachers understanding the principles behind them, teaching becomes performance rather than pedagogy. He presents a five-step framework for shifting to a principles-first approach: name the principle behind each strategy, group strategies into principle families, plan from the principle first, adapt strategies while preserving the principle, and plan the decision the principle sets up. The Chi, Feltovich, and Glaser (1981) novice-expert study is invoked: physics novices sort problems by surface features while experts sort by underlying principles—the same distinction applies to teachers. Clark's closing formulation is the key insight: a strategy without a principle is theatre; a principle without a strategy is a slogan.
points: Strategies are visible teaching actions (cold calling, mini-whiteboards); principles are the learning mechanisms those actions enact (teaching should respond to evidence of student thinking)—and many different strategies can serve the same principle.

When a plan needs to flex mid-lesson, the principle tells you what must be preserved and what can change: adapting a strategy while preserving its principle is responsive teaching; abandoning the principle entirely is drift.

A five-step framework moves teachers from strategy selection to principle-first planning: name the principle, group strategy families, plan from the learning problem first, adapt the strategy while preserving the principle, and decide in advance how you will respond to the evidence the strategy generates.
quotes: Most teachers can name loads of classroom strategies: cold calling, mini-whiteboards, hinge questions, exit tickets, worked examples, retrieval starters, Do Nows, Turn and Talk, choral response.
The strategy is not the pedagogy. The decision is the pedagogy.

Strategies are a roadmap, not the journey. They make effective teaching visible, discussable, and actionable. But the codification of an idea does not improve teaching by itself. In fact, a playbook full of strategies is inert without the principles that give each one its purpose.

A teacher who thinks in strategies organises their practice around mechanical step-by-step processes. A teacher who thinks in principles organises it around what the strategy is designed to achieve. That shift changes how strategies are selected, adapted and combined in classroom practice.
Strategies are how principles get enacted. A strategy without a principle is theatre; a principle without a strategy is a slogan. Teach the principle, and the strategy takes care of itself.
